title: Merge Intervals
statement: Given an array of intervals where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input. Intervals that merely touch — one ending exactly where the next begins — count as overlapping.
realWorld: Building the free/busy view of a calendar: a person's bookings arrive from several sources in no particular order, and the UI needs the blocks of time that are actually occupied. The same routine coalesces adjacent IP ranges, log spans for one incident, and overlapping subtitle windows on a video timeline.

examples.explanation: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap because 2 <= 3, so they become [1,6]. Nothing else overlaps.
They touch at 4. With inclusive ends that counts as overlapping, so they merge.
Both later intervals are contained in [1,10]. The merged end must stay 10 — this is the case that catches a missing Math.max.

constraints: The input is in arbitrary order

bruteForce.idea: Compare every pair. When two overlap, replace them with their union and restart the scan, because the widened interval may now reach something that neither original touched.
code: for (int j = i + 1; j < work.size(); j++) {
if (a[0] <= b[1] && b[0] <= a[1]) {          // the general overlap test
work.set(i, new int[]{ Math.min(a[0], b[0]), Math.max(a[1], b[1]) });
break outer;                             // the set changed; start again
// Presentation only. The merging above never sorts — this puts the finished, disjoint
// blocks into the left-to-right order the answer is printed in.
bruteForce.whySlow: Each scan is O(n^2) and up to n-1 merges each force a fresh scan. The restart is the real tell: because the input is unordered, a merge can create an overlap anywhere, so the code has no idea where to look next and gives up and rechecks everything.

patternIdentification: The moment the input is sorted by start, an interval can only overlap the block currently being built — never anything earlier, since earlier blocks were closed precisely because the current start came after their end, and every later start is larger still. So the pairwise test collapses to one comparison against the last output element, and the whole thing becomes a single pass after an O(n log n) sort.

optimized.idea: Sort by start. Keep the last element of the output list as the open block. Each interval either begins after that block ends — close it, append a new block — or overlaps it, in which case extend its end with `Math.max`. The output comes out sorted for free.
code: // Sort by start: after this, only the open block can still be extended.
merged.add(new int[]{ current[0], current[1] });   // a gap: open a new block
// max, not assignment: [1,10] merged with [3,4] must stay [1,10].

complexity.time: O(n log n) — the sort; the sweep after it is one linear pass
complexity.space: O(n) for the output, plus the sort's own O(log n) to O(n)

code: Arrays.sort(iv, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));   // sort by start
if (out.isEmpty() || cur[0] > out.get(out.size() - 1)[1]) out.add(new int[]{ cur[0], cur[1] });
// otherwise it overlaps the block being built, so stretch that block's end

commonMistakes: Writing `open[1] = current[1]` instead of `Math.max(open[1], current[1])`. A contained interval then shrinks the block, and the staircase test cases that most people try never expose it.
Forgetting to sort, which invalidates the entire 'only the open block can overlap' argument.
Using `>=` for the gap test with inclusive ends, which splits [1,4] and [4,5] into two blocks. The gap test is `current[0] > open[1]`; use `>=` only when ends are exclusive.
Writing the comparator as `(a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]`, which overflows for large or negative bounds. Use `Integer.compare`.
Mutating the input list while iterating it instead of appending to a fresh output list.
Returning `merged.toArray(new int[merged.size()][])` and then indexing it as if it were still sorted by the original input order — sorting has already discarded that order.
